title: Nous Research retrains Alibaba Qwen model, Arete-27B

sources.name: Hugging Face model card, Arete-27B (Nous Research)

verification: Numbers (22% to 0.9%, 803 prompts, 20,000 training prompts, Hermes Bench 65.77 to 65.60, free-expression 60% to 1%, temperature caveat, LLM judge) from the model card; release date about Nov 6 and critics' point from AI Weekly/AITool Ranked/Labmemo summaries. All results are Nous's own; stated as such on the slides.

slides.headline: One retrain cut a Chinese AI's party-line answers to 1%.

image.credit: Photo: Alibaba Group headquarters, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0

slides.text:
An AI lab called Nous Research took Alibaba's open Qwen3.8-27B model and trained it further.
It released the result, Arete-27B, around November 6.

On Nous's own test of 803 questions, 22% of Qwen's answers pushed the official line.
Arete's rate was 0.9%.
On free expression, it fell from 60% to 1%.

image.credit: Photo: Alibaba's Xixi Park campus, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0

slides.text:
How: another AI, called Inkling, wrote model answers to 20,000 prompts on seven themes, including free expression and privacy.
Qwen was then trained on them, about 52.8 million tokens. Nothing else changed.

The catch: Nous graded its own work, using an AI judge.
The two models also ran at different settings. Outside testing has not been reported yet.

image.credit: Illustrative photo: Hangzhou, the city Alibaba is based in, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0

slides.text:
Anyone can download it, with the training data and test questions.
Everything else barely moved: a general benchmark went from 65.77% to 65.60%.
But is tuning an AI toward one set of values neutral?

caption:
A Chinese AI model was retrained, and its answers on sensitive topics changed.

Around November 6, Nous Research released Arete-27B, a version of Alibaba's open Qwen3.8-27B model. Nous says the goal was to cut answers that repeat a state-aligned line on politically sensitive questions.

On its own test of 803 prompts, Nous measured the share of answers containing propaganda. It fell from 22% for Qwen to 0.9% for Arete. On questions about freedom of expression, it went from 60% to 1%. Factual recall on the test rose from 2.32 to 2.98 out of 5.

The method was supervised fine-tuning only. Another AI model, Inkling, wrote answers to 20,000 prompts across seven value categories, and Qwen was trained on them for about 52.8 million tokens. A general benchmark barely changed, from 65.77% to 65.60%.

The caveats are Nous's own. An AI judge graded the answers, the two models ran at different settings, and nobody outside Nous has reported a replication yet. Critics also ask whether steering a model toward one set of values is truly neutral.

The weights, training data and test questions are public.

Would you trust an AI more if it was tuned this way?

Source: Nous Research model card, AI Weekly
